requirements.requirement: Recognition is one part of a therapeutic design; connected formats add separate actions.
The binder and the molecular target it contacts are distinct objects; purple and blue are drawing conventions.
An accessible intended target can occur on cancer and healthy cells; recognition alone gives no tumour exclusivity or safety conclusion.
A binder need not be an entire antibody.
Linking chemical cargo to recognition does not by itself establish entry, processing or usable payload at its action site.
Internalisation is not a universal requirement shared by all of the illustrated formats.
The illustrated soluble T-cell engager has distinct target-recognition and CD3-recognition arms binding different features on separate cells.
Bridging contact alone is not evidence of productive activation or target killing.
The cell-receptor example spans the T-cell membrane and links extracellular recognition to an intracellular signalling design.
A living-cell receptor and a soluble bridging protein are different formats; a floating antibody is not itself a cell receptor.
Function of the assembled product needs testing; receptor anatomy or a signalling symbol is not a measured successful response.
Delivery, function, safety and patient benefit are distinct questions, without a binding-to-benefit progression.
A shared recognition idea does not prove identical module performance after reformatting; the complete product needs tests.
The three designs are illustrative alternatives, not an exhaustive format catalogue, molecular recipe, transformation sequence or efficacy/safety ranking.
In v2 the cargo is drawn outside the cell: the question concerns payload access and is not a depicted successful uptake or release.
In v2 the culture well and blank assay display are measurement cues, with no measured outcome, number or favourable trend.
Shapes, dimensions, quantities, target identity and colours are schematic; the blue target is not a named cancer-only antigen.
The prescribed leader endpoints distinguish binder from target and the CD3 cell feature from the engager arm.
